title: Route 9 Rising
premise: Marguerite Nakamura has spent twelve years being the responsible eldest sibling on Route 9, raising her brother Theo and sister Junie while their mother works hospital nights. When the school's legendary ghost — a student who died in 1979 — begins leaving notes addressed to Marguerite in ink that shouldn't exist, she and her best friend Delia uncover that the ghost's death was ruled an accident to protect a beloved teacher, and that Delia's grandfather was the boy who never spoke up. As the notes multiply and the town's careful silence starts cracking, Marguerite must choose between protecting Delia's family secret and honoring the dead girl's demand for truth. The story ends with the school board reopening the case, Delia testifying against her own blood, and the friendship surviving — changed, scarred, but real — as graduation arrives under a sky that finally feels honest.
about_author: Isandro Halloran is the pen name of a former night-shift dispatcher who grew up in a rust-belt town where everyone knew what happened in 1979 and no one said it aloud. They write young adult fiction about kids who hold families together and the ghosts that hold grudges.

chapters.title: The Careful Years
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. We meet the Nakamura household at 5:40 a.m.: cold cereal, Theo's forgotten permission slip, Junie's braided hair, Mom's night-shift exhaustion. Marguerite runs the house like a drill sergeant because love, in her experience, is logistics. Emotional beat: tenderness disguised as control, and the ache of being twelve years old inside a grown-up's job.

chapters.title: Notes in Impossible Ink
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A note appears taped inside her locker, addressed by name, written in silver ink that shifts color when tilted — the same ink from the legend of the Route 9 ghost, a girl who died in 1979. The janitor swears he locked everything. Emotional beat: eerie wonder cracking open Marguerite's routine, the first thrill of something that isn't her responsibility.

chapters.title: Delia Knows Things
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Delia Vasquez, Marguerite's best friend since kindergarten. Delia goes pale at the mention of the ink and changes the subject hard. That night she burns something in her backyard barrel. Emotional beat: the first hairline fracture in the friendship; Marguerite notices and files it away, careful as always.

chapters.title: The Legend According to Everyone
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, comic relief turning serious. Theo interviews classmates for a history project about 'the girl in the stairwell' and collects four contradictory versions of her death. He brings them home like trophies. Emotional beat: Theo's brightness masking his own fear of being the kid nobody takes seriously; Marguerite realizes the town's memory is a patchwork of convenient lies.

chapters.title: Second Note, First Name
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A second note names not just Marguerite but Junie — 'tell your sister she hums the same song.' The song is one their mother sings. The ghost knows their family. Marguerite lies to Mom for the first time in years. Emotional beat: dread replacing wonder; the supernatural has reached into the one thing Marguerite protects most.

chapters.title: Yearbook, 1979
chapters.summary: Marguerite and Delia's joint POV, told in alternating sections. In the library archive they find the yearbook: Rosalind Okonkwo, honor roll, choir, gone mid-spring. Beside her photo, a teacher's name — Mr. Aldous Wren — circled in that same shifting ink. Delia flinches at the name. Emotional beat: the past becoming specific, human, and dangerous; Delia's guilt leaking through the seams.

chapters.title: What Grandfather Buried
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Delia finds a shoebox in her grandfather Emilio's closet: a choir program, a crushed corsage, and an unsent letter beginning 'Rosalind, I should have said.' She confronts him; he weeps and says only, 'Wren told us what to say.' Emotional beat: inherited silence as a family heirloom; Delia torn between loyalty to a dying old man and a dead girl who won't stop writing.

chapters.title: Junie Hums It Too
chapters.summary: Junie's POV, age nine, matter-of-fact and unnerving. Junie admits she learned the song from a lady who visits her dreams, 'the one with the ribbon in her hair.' She describes the stairwell landing exactly. Emotional beat: childhood clarity cutting through adult evasion; Marguerite's protective instinct colliding with the fact that Junie isn't afraid.

chapters.title: The Third Note Is a Map
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A note arrives with hand-drawn directions to the sealed sub-basement beneath the gym, plus a warning: 'Bring the Vasquez girl or don't come.' Marguerite must ask Delia for help without revealing she knows about the shoebox. Emotional beat: two friends lying by omission in perfect sync, each convinced she's protecting the other.

chapters.title: Below the Gymnasium
chapters.summary: Joint POV. They slip in during Saturday detention coverage and find the old choir room: water-stained walls, a piano with one working key, and chalk lines still marking where chairs stood in 1979. On the piano, a fresh note: 'He said I fell. I did not fall.' Emotional beat: awe curdling into grief; the room is a wound the building grew around.

chapters.title: Mom Works Nights
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, interwoven with a phone call home. Mom, exhausted between shifts, reveals a fragment: she transferred into this district in the eighties and remembers when 'the Wren scholarship' was quietly renamed. She warns Marguerite, without knowing why, 'Some truths cost more than they pay.' Emotional beat: Marguerite realizing her mother chose this town's silence too — and that care can be its own kind of complicity.

chapters.title: Wren Still Teaches Here
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo discovers that Mr. Wren didn't just teach in 1979 — he retired last spring and still runs the alumni fund, beloved, photographed, plaque on the wall. Theo innocently asks him about Rosalind for his project and watches the old man's face go to stone. Emotional beat: the villain revealed not as a monster but as a respected institution; Theo's first taste of adult fear.

chapters.title: The Friendship Fracture
chapters.summary: Dual POV collision. Marguerite confronts Delia about the letter; Delia accuses Marguerite of using the ghost to escape her own life, of wanting a drama bigger than dishes and permission slips. Both say unforgivable-adjacent things. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh — loyalty demanding silence, truth demanding betrayal — and neither girl wrong enough to be the villain.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Being Careful
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, quiet chapter. Alone at 2 a.m., Marguerite audits her life: every party missed, every secret kept, every time she swallowed a truth to keep the household steady. She writes a list titled 'Things I Have Never Said' and it runs three pages. Emotional beat: the midpoint mirror; Marguerite sees that the ghost's demand is also her own unfinished business.

chapters.title: Emilio Confesses
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Grandfather Emilio, hospitalized after a fall, finally tells the whole story: Wren cornered Rosalind in the stairwell over stolen exam answers Wren himself planted; she fell; the boys who saw it were fed a story and scholarships. Emilio kept his. Emotional beat: confession as both relief and detonation; Delia now holds the evidence that will destroy her family's name.

chapters.title: The Notes Stop
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The ink notes cease. The stairwell feels ordinary. Junie says the dream lady 'sounds tired now, like she's almost done.' Marguerite panics — the truth is half-told and the witness is fading. Emotional beat: the horror of a cause going quiet before justice arrives; urgency replacing fear.

chapters.title: Alumni Night
chapters.summary: Full-cast chapter, rotating close-third among all three siblings. At the school's alumni gala honoring Wren's fifty-year legacy, Theo hacks the slideshow, Junie slips the original unsent letter into the program folders, and Marguerite stands up during the toast and reads Rosalind's final note aloud: 'I did not fall.' Emotional beat: the climax — courage performed publicly, irreversibly, by three kids who were never supposed to be in the room.

chapters.title: The Fallout
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. The town splits: some call Marguerite a liar chasing attention; others come forward with memories they'd carried for forty years. Wren resigns from the fund. Delia's grandfather, watching the news, tells her he's proud — the first time those words have ever landed clean. Emotional beat: chaos, backlash, and the strange lightness of having nothing left to hide.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The school board reopens the case; Delia testifies against her own family name, voice shaking, holding Emilio's letter. Marguerite sits beside her though they haven't spoken in weeks. Emotional beat: loyalty redefined — not agreement, but presence; the friendship's rebirth begins in a fluorescent-lit hearing room.

chapters.title: One Last Note
chapters.summary: Junie's POV. A final note appears, addressed to all three Nakamura children: 'Thank you for saying it out loud. You can put me down now.' The ink fades permanently. Junie reports the dream lady smiled and left. Emotional beat: release and gentle sorrow; the ghost was never a haunting, only a request.

chapters.title: Graduation Weather
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Spring: a plaque for Rosalind Okonkwo goes up by the stairwell, worded honestly. Mom picks up extra day shifts so she can actually be home at dinner. Marguerite delivers her valedictory-adjacent speech about the difference between keeping people safe and keeping them silent. Emotional beat: earned hope; the careful years ending not with rebellion but with integration.

chapters.title: Route 9, Going Forward
chapters.summary: Ensemble epilogue, brief passages from Marguerite, Delia, Theo, and Junie. Summer on Route 9: Delia and Marguerite repaint the choir room together as volunteers, Theo wins the history fair with the true version, Junie hums a new song. Final image: the three of them on the porch as Mom's car pulls in before dark. Emotional beat: found family solidified into real family; truth survived, and so did they.
